# Maria's Morning Route

Maria has been driving the same bus route through the city for twenty-three years. She knows every pothole on Mercado Street, every corner where the afternoon sun glares through the windshield, every regular passenger by name. Her husband, Roberto, jokes that she could drive the route in her sleep. But Maria hasn't slept well in fourteen months.

It started on an ordinary Tuesday in March. Maria was approaching the downtown transit hub around 8:45 in the morning, her bus about two-thirds full with the usual commuters. A young man—she remembers he couldn't have been more than twenty—stumbled onto the bus at the last stop before the hub. He was agitated, sweating, his eyes moving rapidly from passenger to passenger. Maria noticed immediately because she always notices. In her job, you develop a certain awareness.

She asked him gently if he was okay, if he needed help. He didn't answer. Instead, he pulled a knife from his jacket and lunged at the elderly woman sitting directly behind Maria's seat—Mrs. Chen, who took the same route every Tuesday and Thursday to visit her daughter. The blade caught Mrs. Chen across the neck and shoulder. There was blood immediately, shocking in its brightness against Mrs. Chen's beige cardigan.

Maria's hands were gripping the steering wheel. She couldn't move. Later, she would replay this moment hundreds of times, wondering if she should have done something differently, though logically she knew there was nothing she could have done. The other passengers screamed. Someone called 911. Maria sat frozen, still holding the wheel, while Mrs. Chen made a sound—not quite a scream, something rawer—and pressed her hand to her neck.

The ambulance came. The police came. Mrs. Chen survived, though she required surgery and didn't take the bus for months afterward. Maria gave her statement and went home at noon, something she'd never done in twenty-three years.

Now, fourteen months later, Maria still drives the route. She tells herself she cannot let fear win, cannot let one terrible moment define her career or her life. This is what she tells Roberto, and it's partly true. But the truth is more complicated. Every morning before her shift, her stomach tightens. Every passenger who boards quickly or moves unexpectedly sends a jolt through her chest. She finds herself watching hands more than faces, tracking every person's position relative to others. Her shoulders stay tense throughout her shift.

She's stopped taking breaks at the transit hub. She eats her lunch in the bus now, doors locked, watching the parking lot through the mirror. She's hyperaware of sounds—a raised voice, a bag being unzipped too quickly, the scrape of a shoe on the floor. Last week, a teenager dropped a metal can near the back of the bus, and Maria's heart raced so hard she had to pull over, pretending to check the tire pressure while she waited for her breathing to slow.

Roberto has noticed she's different. She's snappish in the mornings, irritable in ways she wasn't before. She doesn't enjoy their evening walks anymore—she's too alert, too tense. At night, she lies awake thinking about Mrs. Chen, about the sound of that knife, about all the people who ride her bus every day, and all the terrible things that could happen that she cannot prevent.

She loves her job. She still loves her job. But something in her has fractured, and she doesn't know how to put it back together.
